title: Explain a delay
scenario: A bug may delay your group’s feature. Your project leader is not technical and asks for an update.

options.text: Send the error logs and describe which functions failed.
Explain the impact, your next step, and when you will provide another update.
Wait until you have a complete fix before giving an update.
Report the delay and ask a teammate to explain the details.

title: Clarify a request
scenario: A classmate asks you to “make the dashboard better.” You are unsure what they want changed.

options.text: Suggest a visual redesign and ask them to review it afterward.
Ask which task is difficult and confirm a specific example of the desired improvement.
Ask them to write a full specification before discussing the request.
Make the changes that your group has requested most often before.

title: Share a technical finding
scenario: Your group needs to understand why a website is slow. You have collected several technical measurements.

options.text: Present all measurements so the group has the complete picture.
Summarize the main finding, explain its effect, and offer details for follow-up questions.
Share only the solution you prefer to keep the discussion short.
Send a tutorial on website performance before the meeting.

title: Recover a missed handoff
scenario: A teammate misses a deadline, blocking your part of the group project. There is still time to adjust the plan.

options.text: Complete their part yourself and explain the change at the next meeting.
Discuss the blocker privately, agree on a recovery plan, and update the group’s timeline.
Ask the leader to reassign their tasks before you speak to them.
Continue your available tasks and wait for their update.

title: Work through disagreement
scenario: Two teammates disagree about which framework to use. Both approaches meet the project requirements.

options.text: Ask each to compare the options against agreed criteria, then help the group decide.
Vote immediately so the group can return to building.
Support the teammate who has the most experience.
Prototype both complete approaches before making any decision.

title: Balance participation
scenario: One teammate rarely speaks during planning meetings, but submits thoughtful written ideas afterward.

options.text: Ask for their view ahead of the next meeting and make space for it in the discussion.
Explain that ideas need to be raised during the meeting to count.
Assign them individual tasks so they do not need to participate in planning.
Share their written ideas yourself to keep the meeting moving.

title: Investigate an unfamiliar issue
scenario: A feature fails on one laptop but works on the others. You do not know the cause yet.

options.text: Reinstall the project dependencies on every laptop.
Compare the error, steps to reproduce, and environment before testing a focused explanation.
Ask the affected teammate to use another laptop for now.
Change the most recently edited function and check whether it helps.

title: Check conflicting evidence
scenario: A user reports missing records, but your first test shows all records are present.

options.text: Close the report because your test passed.
Ask for the user’s exact steps and compare their filters and permissions with your test.
Restore an older database backup to recover the missing records.
Tell the user to refresh and report again if the problem continues.

title: Choose a practical next step
scenario: Your group has several ideas for fixing a recurring issue, but little time to investigate.

options.text: Choose the quickest change and deploy it immediately.
Compare impact and evidence, then run a small reversible test of the most promising explanation.
Research every possible cause before trying a change.
Implement the solution used by a similar project without further checks.

title: Respond to feedback
scenario: Your instructor says the prototype is difficult for beginners to navigate. You invested considerable time in its current design.

options.text: Explain the design decisions and keep the interface until more people complain.
Ask for examples, observe a beginner trying it, and revise the most important obstacles.
Replace the entire design immediately to show you accepted the feedback.
Ask a teammate to handle the feedback while you continue your planned tasks.

title: Handle a changed requirement
scenario: A project requirement changes halfway through development. Your group has a fixed submission date.

options.text: Keep the original plan and explain the change was too late.
Clarify the new priority, assess its effect, and agree on a revised scope with the group.
Add the new requirement while keeping every existing commitment.
Start implementing the change before discussing its effect on other tasks.

title: Learn a new tool
scenario: Your team needs a tool you have not used before. A small task is due soon, and support is available.

options.text: Ask someone experienced to complete your task while you watch.
Learn the essentials, try a small example, and seek focused help where you get stuck.
Complete a full course before attempting the task.
Use your familiar tool without checking whether its output meets the team’s needs.
